clue.text: Clubs worker's sacked, caught breaking bottle opener

indicators.note: a sacked place has been ransacked and turned upside down, so these letters are thrown into disorder
something breaking into a group pushes inside it, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for clubs, the card suit
the letters of the word, ignoring the apostrophe
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A nightclub employee is fired after being caught smashing a bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in "worker's" is ignored, so the seven letters of WORKERS are rearranged and the cricket C for caught is dropped into the middle, after the Clubs C at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: The spiral tool used to pull corks out of wine is the classic device for uncorking a bottle.

clue.text: Church gathering incorporated piece of cake

indicators.note: to gather something in is to draw it into yourself, so one piece is enclosed by another

blocks.note: CH is the standard abbreviation for church
Inc. is the abbreviation used after American company names

explanation.surface: A church social where someone has brought along a slice of cake.
explanation.walkthrough: "Church gathering" reads as a congregation meeting, but gathering is a verb here: the church abbreviation gathers the company one inside itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal phrases for a task that is very easy to do, needing no effort at all.

clue.text: Redo short haircut for swimmer

indicators.note: something cut short has lost its end, so the final letter is removed

blocks.note: taken as written
a mullet is the hairstyle short at the front and long at the back

explanation.surface: Someone asks the barber to redo a short haircut.
explanation.walkthrough: "Short haircut" looks like one phrase, but short belongs to Redo, trimming its last letter; the haircut is the famous mullet.
explanation.definitionFit: This reddish Mediterranean fish is a sea creature, and crossword setters often call any fish a swimmer.

clue.text: Film star rocks party, wearing nothing

indicators.note: a wearer sits inside the clothes, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: scree is loose broken rock on a mountain slope
nil means nothing, as in a football score
a do is an informal word for a party

explanation.surface: A celebrity rocks up to a party wearing no clothes at all.
explanation.walkthrough: "Rocks" looks like a verb about partying hard, but it is the noun for loose stones on a hillside. A wearer sits inside the clothes, so the party goes inside nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A celebrated cinema actor adored by fans is a star of the silver screen, idolised by the public.

clue.text: Teach new skills online

blocks.note: split as on + line: re means on or concerning, as in a letter heading
a train is a line of people or things following one another

explanation.surface: An online course that teaches people new skills.
explanation.walkthrough: "Online" must be split into its two words, on and line, which give the two parts in order.
explanation.definitionFit: To train someone again in different work is to give them fresh abilities for a new job.

clue.text: Most desolate quarter has listed building

indicators.note: building means constructing, so these letters are put together in a new form

blocks.note: W for west, one of the four compass quarters
taken as written

explanation.surface: The bleakest part of town contains a listed building.
explanation.walkthrough: "Listed building" is a fixed British phrase for a protected historic building, but here it splits: listed is the fodder and building tells you to rearrange it. A quarter is a compass point, N, S, E or W.
explanation.definitionFit: Wild land is barren, uncultivated and untamed, so the superlative describes the most desolate terrain.

clue.text: Natural gemstones not right for rings

indicators.note: saying something is not there tells you to take it out

blocks.note: pearls grow naturally in oysters
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A jeweller choosing natural stones, but not the right ones, for wedding rings.
explanation.walkthrough: "Rings" looks like jewellery to go with the gemstones, but it is the sound of bells.
explanation.definitionFit: A peal is a loud ringing of bells, so the plural noun matches the noun rings in that sense.

clue.text: Brace for party leader broadcast

indicators.note: a leader comes at the front, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
to air a programme is to broadcast it

explanation.surface: Getting ready for a party leader's televised speech.
explanation.walkthrough: "Party leader" suggests a politician, but it only means the first letter of party.
explanation.definitionFit: A brace is two of something, especially game birds shot together, so it is another word for a couple.

clue.text: Regular guest is host for debate

indicators.note: a host has someone staying within, so the words contain the letters needed

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A frequent guest on a TV programme hosts a debate.
explanation.walkthrough: "Regular" suggests taking every other letter, but the letters run straight through, across the word break.
explanation.definitionFit: To debate is to dispute a point with someone, putting reasons for and against a position.

clue.text: Day before American artist's retrospective, it's blocked

indicators.note: a retrospective looks back, so everything is read from the end

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for day
ere is an old word for before
Jeff Koons is the American artist famous for balloon dog sculptures

explanation.surface: The day before an American artist's retrospective exhibition, the gallery is closed off.
explanation.walkthrough: A retrospective is an exhibition of an artist's career, but here it reverses the whole chain of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: In snooker a player is blocked from hitting the target ball, and the idiom extends to anyone thwarted or obstructed.

clue.text: Detective managed to retire without getting to rock bottom

indicators.note: to retire is to draw back, so the letters go backwards
without in its old sense of outside, so one piece wraps around another

blocks.note: to run a business is to manage it
DI is a Detective Inspector

explanation.surface: A detective who managed to retire without ever hitting rock bottom in life.
explanation.walkthrough: "Without" here means outside, not lacking: the reversed word goes around the detective.
explanation.definitionFit: The nadir is the lowest point of anything, literally the point of the sky directly below an observer.

clue.text: Carpeting tripped tot heading off toddling inside

indicators.note: someone who has tripped is sent sprawling, so these letters land in a jumbled order
with its heading off, a word loses its first letter
inside places one piece within another

blocks.note: taken as written
to toddle is to walk unsteadily like a small child

explanation.surface: A toddler trips on the carpet while learning to walk.
explanation.walkthrough: "Carpeting" seems to be floor covering, but to carpet someone is British slang for to reprimand them. The beheaded walk sits inside the shuffled tot.
explanation.definitionFit: Being carpeted means getting a stern telling-off from a boss, so the noun names that scolding.

clue.text: Dislikes trapping poor mouse for co-residents

indicators.note: something in poor shape is broken down, so these letters are rearranged
to trap something is to hold it inside, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: to hate is to dislike strongly
taken as written

explanation.surface: Flatmates who dislike setting traps for a poor little mouse.
explanation.walkthrough: "Poor" reads as pity for the mouse, but it signals rearranging its letters before they go inside the word for dislikes.
explanation.definitionFit: People who share a house, living under one roof together, are the residents of that home with you.

clue.text: Wally's quick rejoinder partly backfired

indicators.note: partly means only a portion of the words is used, sitting inside them
something that backfires comes back the wrong way, so the letters run in reverse

blocks.note: the letters straddle the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: A fool's snappy comeback goes wrong and rebounds on him.
explanation.walkthrough: A wally is British slang for a silly, foolish person.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal insults for a stupid or contemptible person, the American term matching the British one.

clue.text: Indulged by wearing uniforms I'd later bother keeping

indicators.note: a wearer sits inside the clothes, so one piece goes within another
to bother something is to disturb it, so these letters are stirred up
to keep something is to hold it inside, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: X is the multiplication sign, read as by in measurements like 3 by 4
U is Uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet, and there are two of them
the letters of the words, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone indulged themselves in wearing uniforms and will deal with it later.
explanation.walkthrough: Plural uniforms gives two Us, with the multiplication sign worn between them; that little cluster then sits inside the scrambled letters after the first.
explanation.definitionFit: To luxuriate is to take great pleasure in comfort, wallowing in it, so the past tense means treated oneself.

clue.text: Large number of British having trouble at home with nothing coming in

indicators.note: coming in means entering, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for British
ill as a noun means harm or trouble
someone at home is in
the figure zero looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: Huge numbers of Britons struggling at home with no income arriving.
explanation.walkthrough: "Nothing coming in" sounds like lack of money, but it tells you to put the zero letter into the word for at home.
explanation.definitionFit: A billion, a thousand million, is a very big figure, and the word is often used loosely for any huge quantity.

clue.text: Falsely superior large loaf has seeds occasionally

indicators.note: occasionally means now and then, so only every other letter is kept

blocks.note: big means large
loaf is slang for head, as in use your loaf, from rhyming slang loaf of bread
the second and fourth letters of the word

explanation.surface: A smug baker shows off a big seeded loaf.
explanation.walkthrough: "Loaf" looks like bread to go with the seeds, but it is the slang word for head.
explanation.definitionFit: A bigheaded person is conceited, believing themselves better than others without good reason.

clue.text: So distant up to now

blocks.note: thus means so, as in and so
far means distant

explanation.surface: A traveller remarks on how remote a place is.
explanation.walkthrough: "So distant" reads as one phrase meaning very far away, but each word gives its own synonym and the last three words are the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means until this point in time, as in progress has been slow so far.

clue.text: The lift is out of order, being most dirty

indicators.note: things out of order are not in their proper sequence, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A broken-down lift in a grimy block of flats is the dirtiest place around.
explanation.walkthrough: "Out of order" is the natural sign on a broken lift, which disguises its job of rearranging the three words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Filthy means very dirty, and its superlative form is the dirtiest of all.

clue.text: Let's go travelling, tour's beginning on your bike

indicators.note: something travelling moves around, so these letters shift into a new order
the beginning of a word is its first letter, which is all that is kept

blocks.note: the letters of the words, ignoring the apostrophe
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A cyclist urging friends to set off on a bike tour.
explanation.walkthrough: "On your bike" is a British phrase telling someone to go away, not an instruction to ride.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are rude, informal ways of telling someone to leave at once and stop bothering you.

clue.text: Time opponent's taken over me is not significant

indicators.note: a firm taken over is absorbed, so one piece swallows another

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
a rival is an opponent
I is how a speaker refers to me as a subject

explanation.surface: The time my opponent has spent beating me hardly matters.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe s in "opponent's" stands for has: the rival has taken over the speaker, enclosing a letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Something trivial is unimportant and of little value or consequence.

clue.text: Almost everything eaten by sea creature's foul!

indicators.note: almost all of something is missing its last bit, so the final letter is dropped
something eaten ends up inside the eater, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: a squid is a ten-armed sea creature
all means everything

explanation.surface: A sea creature that eats nearly everything in sight is disgusting!
explanation.walkthrough: The trimmed word for everything goes inside the many-armed creature.
explanation.definitionFit: Squalid means filthy and unpleasant, especially from neglect, so it shares the sense of disgusting.

clue.text: Detectives in violent tussle seizing drug

indicators.note: violent action throws things about, so these letters are scrambled
to seize something is to grab hold of it, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: taken as written
H is slang for heroin

explanation.surface: Police officers in a violent scuffle while confiscating drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: H for heroin is a common crossword shorthand for drug.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleuth is an informal, slightly old-fashioned word for a detective or investigator.

clue.text: Thin line moving between English and American style

indicators.note: a piece that is moving leaves its place, so it comes out of the word first
between puts a piece inside a gap, so it ends up enclosed

blocks.note: lean means thin
L is the abbreviation for line
E for English and A for American name the two letters the moved letter lands between; they are already there

explanation.surface: A thin line drawn between English and American style.
explanation.walkthrough: The line letter leaves the front of the word for thin and reinserts itself between the E and the A already inside, so English and American add no letters of their own.
explanation.definitionFit: Elan is flair and dash, a confident stylishness in how something is done.

clue.text: Terrible fellow you reportedly left after a week

indicators.note: reportedly means as people say, so the word is taken by its sound
after means the pieces that follow are placed later in the answer

blocks.note: taken as written
W is the abbreviation for week
F is the abbreviation for fellow
the letter U is said just like you
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A dreadful man, so people say, walked out on you after only a week.
explanation.walkthrough: Every piece is a single letter, and "after" means the three from the start of the clue go behind the last two.
explanation.definitionFit: Awful and terrible are synonyms, both meaning very bad or unpleasant.

clue.text: Team weakens, stuffed with southern hotel's extra food

indicators.note: something stuffed has a filling packed inside it

blocks.note: a side is a team in sport
a sound that dies away weakens and fades
S is the abbreviation for southern
H is Hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A sports team flags after gorging on a southern hotel's extra food.
explanation.walkthrough: "Stuffed" suggests overeating, but it means the word for weakens is filled with the two abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: Side dishes are extra items served alongside a main course, such as salad or chips.

clue.text: Mum's quiet after son in car accident

indicators.note: after means those pieces are placed later in the answer

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for son
ma is an informal word for mother
sh is the instruction to be quiet

explanation.surface: A mother falls silent after her son is involved in a car crash.
explanation.walkthrough: "In" joins the wordplay to the definition at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A smash is an informal word for a road collision, especially a violent one.

clue.text: Rejected new street map that's variable and eccentric

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for new
the A-Z is a British book of street maps, best known for London
y is a standard algebraic variable

explanation.surface: Someone throws out a new street map as unreliable and odd.
explanation.walkthrough: "Variable" looks like an adjective describing the map, but it is a noun: an algebra letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Zany means amusingly unconventional and wacky, so it matches eccentric in the sense of odd behaviour.

clue.text: One with no hope of French act winning

blocks.note: de is French for of
a feat is a notable act or deed
a winner comes 1st, written with the digit 1 read as the letter I

explanation.surface: A pessimist doubts the French act has any chance of winning a contest.
explanation.walkthrough: "Of" belongs to the definition-looking phrase but is part of the wordplay, translated into French. Winning is first place, 1st, with the numeral read as a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A defeatist is a person who expects failure and gives up too easily, so has no optimism.

clue.text: Letter from Greece is first of hundreds in Tate collection

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter, which is all that is kept
a collection gathers things up together, so these letters are assembled in a new order

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
taken as written; the Tate is a group of London art galleries

explanation.surface: A letter sent from Greece is the pick of hundreds held in the Tate gallery's collection.
explanation.walkthrough: "Tate collection" sounds like the art gallery's holdings, but collection tells you to rearrange the name with the extra letter put in.
explanation.definitionFit: Theta is the eighth character of the Greek alphabet, the one written like an O with a bar.

clue.text: Hang around with dopehead's mate

indicators.note: a head is at the top, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: split as dope + head: the opening letter of dope
an ally is a friend or supporter

explanation.surface: Spending time loafing about with a stoner's friend.
explanation.walkthrough: "Dopehead" reads as one slang word for a drug user, but it splits into dope and head, meaning its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To dally is to waste time or dawdle, so it means loitering without purpose.

clue.text: Endure, long after date that's absolutely final

indicators.note: after means those pieces are placed later in the answer

blocks.note: to last is to endure or keep going
D is the abbreviation for date
to itch for something is to long for it

explanation.surface: Holding on, yearning beyond the deadline for something truly final.
explanation.walkthrough: "Long" is a verb meaning to yearn, not an adjective about length.
explanation.definitionFit: A last-ditch effort is a final desperate attempt, made when every other option has failed.
